 + Follow on Google Add as preferred source SC stay puts advocate-client privilege at the heart of GST searches 
 The Supreme Court on September 28 stayed the Delhi High Court verdict of September 18, which had upheld the GST Department’s search and seizure of advocate Puneet Batra’s office computers. The issue is whether, despite fiduciary or privileged relationships not being sacrosanct and authorities being entitled to probe beyond what is apparent on the surface, seizing an advocate’s computers could compromise privileged information belonging to other clients. This risk is heightened by the absence of a Chinese wall to segregate one client’s confidential information from that of another.
 The GST counsel said it will redact the information pertaining to other clients. Redaction is the process of removing or obscuring sensitive, confidential, or private information from a document before it is published or shared publicly. It remains to be seen how far that is feasible. The dispute stems from a GST search conducted on July 25, 2025, at the premises of Bass Legal LLP, including Batra’s cabin. 
 The authorities seized his CPU, documents and other material during the operation. The search was conducted under Section 67(2) of the Central GST Act, 2017. According to the High Court record, Batra had been providing professional services to Martkarma Technology Pvt Ltd (MTPL), a gaming company, since 2023. His work for the company was stated to include GST and other tax matters, corporate compliance, income-tax and TDS returns, intellectual property work, trademark registration and cyber-crime-related matters.
 The GST authorities, however, alleged that his role went beyond providing legal advice and that he had become involved in the affairs and operations of the company under investigation. The last word hasn’t been spoken yet on the issue. The case will be watched very closely by the legal fraternity.
 Order Giving Effect is a must 
 In Global Hospitality Licensing SARL v. Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Income-tax (International Taxation), the Hon’ble Bombay High Court was called upon to decide whether an Assessing Officer’s failure to pass an Order Giving Effect within the prescribed statutory period would render the assessment proceedings, and the consequential penalty, legally unsustainable.
 The judgment has wider implications for both taxpayers and the Income Tax Department in that a bland order without a subsequent order giving effect is of no use. By holding that the failure to pass an Order Giving Effect within the limitation prescribed under Section 153 results in the abatement of the assessment proceedings, the Court also made it clear that any consequential penalty cannot be sustained in law.
 An Order Giving Effect is the order passed by the Assessing Officer to implement the directions contained in an appellate order. It gives practical effect to the appellate decision by recomputing the tax liability, determining the final demand or refund, and carrying out any consequential directions. In other words, it provides the nuts and bolts of the in-principle order.
 Compensation in the course of business is business income 
 The Bombay bench of Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) recently said agreement termination compensation received by Marico Industries without causing damage to its capital structure constitutes business income under Section 28 of the Income-tax Act. Compensation for terminating a routine commercial agreement is treated as revenue receipt. The ruling applies when the termination does not impair or damage the core profit-making apparatus or capital structure of the business.
 Tax authorities classify such inflows under Section 28 as normal trading or business profits rather than capital gains. The questions to be asked are was it a routine operational contract or a foundational capital asset? Did the cancellation paralyze overall business infrastructure or just a commercial arrangement? If the answers are routine and not foundational and did not paralyze overall business, it is a routine operation and hence the compensation is incidental to business and hence a revenue receipt.
 — The author, S Murlidharan is a Chartered Accountant, and interprets tax-related rulings and judgments in this column. The views expressed are personal.
